title: Professional power: AI redistributes tasks and status
desc: Uses organizational and sociological perspectives to explain defended judgment domains, multidisciplinary work and contested professional exclusivity.

kps.k: AI changes legal work through organisational choices and professional power, not technical capability alone.
kps.d: The cluster shifts the debate from whether machines replace lawyers to how firms and professions organise changing work. Faulconbridge’s mediated evolution framework describes meaningful but non-linear change shaped by existing practices, autonomy and partnership governance. Faulconbridge, Sarwar and Spring explain accommodation as professionals justifying adoption while addressing technological limitations. Armour and Sako add that business models, human expertise and technological assets jointly determine substitution, augmentation and new-task creation. These accounts reject both an unchanged profession and an inevitable technological endpoint.

qs.q: Through the analysis the paper develops the concept of mediated evolution which is a way of conceptualising change in legal work that is material and meaningful, but which is also path dependent and non-linear and thus needs to be understood through situated analysis of the enactment in practice of change.
qs.a: Trajectories of legal work in the context of machine learning AI: conceptualising mediated evolution · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Accommodating machine learning algorithms is comprised of recursive processes enabled by the way professionals themselves control both how machine learning algorithms are incorporated into work and how work organization evolves in PSFs.
qs.a: Accommodating Machine Learning Algorithms in Professional Service Firms · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Professionals can surrender selected tasks while defending valued judgement and expanding their advisory domains.
kps.d: In their 2018–2020 qualitative research, Faulconbridge, Sarwar and Spring find intertwined boundary work: accountants and lawyers delegate some collation and review, restate claims to bespoke judgement, and use newly affordable data analysis to develop services. They report professional reconfiguration without mass redundancies at that time, not immunity from future displacement. Faulconbridge’s separate account reports slow, compartmentalised adoption concentrated on cost-saving automation. Participants’ claims that lawyers using AI outperform either alone explain how they legitimise new roles; they do not establish comparative performance.

qs.q: The defining of new domains was made possible by the ability of AI-­driven systems to analyse datasets that were previously too costly or slow to review (see Table II), the data analysis then being used by professionals to offer new forms of advisory services relating to a range of client concerns.
qs.a: How Professionals Adapt to Artificial Intelligence: The Role of Intertwined Boundary Work · Academia · 2023

qs.q: (2023), found slow and often compartmentalised adoption restricted to one team or practice group and mainly the automation aspects of ML being used, as part of cost-saving efforts, with some of the more advanced augmentation possibilities yet to emerge.
qs.a: Trajectories of legal work in the context of machine learning AI: conceptualising mediated evolution · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Multidisciplinary collaboration redistributes work, status and influence within firms.
kps.d: Augmented Lawyering distinguishes lawyers who use AI-enabled services in advice from legal experts who help produce those services with other specialists. The boundary-work research finds technologists contributing insights, gaining partnership access and influencing work organisation—not merely receiving low-status tasks. Sako, Qian and Attolini distinguish protective control, which delegates to subordinate occupations, from connective control, which permits equal-status collaboration. Their job-posting study reports support through comparisons across British and US settings, organisational forms and sectors, although the supplied abstract gives no estimates. Whether these roles require full lawyer qualification remains open.

qs.q: First, we offer an integrated anal- ysis of the different margins along which AI will impact legal services work: substitution for some tasks; augmentation of human lawyers who consume AI- enabled services; and augmentation by humans with legal expertise of the pro- duction of these AI-enabled services.
qs.a: Augmented Lawyering · Academia · 2022

qs.q: In our analysis this relates to how technologists gain access to the partnership and begin to influence control over how professional work is organized.
qs.a: How Professionals Adapt to Artificial Intelligence: The Role of Intertwined Boundary Work · Academia · 2023

kps.k: The governance debate concerns organisational fit and human coordination, not simply access to capital.
kps.d: Armour and Sako’s 2020 theoretical account suggests that corporate structures better complement scalable, output-priced AI services through centralised management, outside capital and employee incentives. Augmented Lawyering’s 2022 empirical account places the main implementation difficulty elsewhere: lawyer-only partnerships struggle to recruit, motivate and coordinate multidisciplinary teams rather than raise capital. Its UK cases nevertheless support a continuing economic rationale for advisory partnerships that mainly consume AI services. The practical choices include contracting, integrating production internally, or running old and new models in parallel; the evidence does not establish one universally superior form.

qs.q: Third, we analyse the organizational structure that complements the old and new business models: the professional partnership (P2) is well- adapted to delivering the legal advisory business model, but the centralized management, access to outside capital and employee incentives offered by the corporate form appear better to complement the new AI-enabled business models.
qs.a: AI-enabled business models in legal services: from traditional law firms to next-generation law companies? · Academia · 2020

qs.q: Third, our empirical findings contrasting the deployment of AI-enabled legal services in different types of organization show that the challenges for lawyer-only partnerships in implementing AI lie not in capital constraints, but in the difficulties in coordi- nating the human side of the process—recruiting and motivating MDTs.
qs.a: Augmented Lawyering · Academia · 2022

kps.k: Human judgement may gain value, but its continuing exclusivity and employment effects remain disputed.
kps.d: Becoming the AI-Enhanced Lawyer reasons that better prediction increases the relative value of judgement about what to do; Flood and Robb predict renewed importance for trusted advice. Other contributions qualify this division: complex work can be automatable, and Bell and Rogers argue that GenAI reaches activities central to developing and displaying expertise, making isolated task-replacement models less applicable. The Evolution of Legal Knowledge Work suggests that codifying knowledge in data and playbooks could shift value and control from individuals to firms. Advisory roles may persist while fewer broadly capable lawyers are needed; alternatively, increased demand for augmented services may offset substitution. Neither employment outcome is established.

qs.q: While given the right conditions AI may be better at ‘prediction’, judgement is required to know what to do with the prediction.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence and the Legal Profession: Becoming the AI-Enhanced Lawyer · Academia · 2019

qs.q: Using examples from law, such as Gulati           and Scott’s analysis of how lawyers create (or don’t create)           legal agreements, we show that even non-routine and com-           plex legal work is potentially susceptible to automation.
qs.a: Professions and Expertise: How Machine Learning and Blockchain Are Redesigning the Landscape of Professional Knowledge and Organization · Academia · 2019

kps.k: Immediate assistance can coexist with risks to learning, interpretation and professional identity.
kps.d: The generative-machine-learning research agenda distinguishes improved outputs from the development of practical expertise: benchmarks can omit know-how, and unreflective reliance on opaque outputs may weaken experiential learning. Interviews with 18 legal professionals in Reimagining Legal Fact Verification report reduced manual burden alongside concerns that AI shapes initial factual understanding and interrupts development of professional intuition. These are qualitative accounts, not measured deskilling. Bell and Rogers extend the issue to socialisation, mentoring and entrants’ motivation. Practical implications include preserving scrutiny, reflection and human development alongside tool adoption, rather than treating productivity gains as proof that training remains effective.

kps.k: Professional adaptation raises public-accountability questions as well as questions of occupational survival.
kps.d: Bell and Rogers connect professional identity to the bargain exchanging autonomy and rewards for ethical, competent service. They warn conditionally that devalued expertise, bypassed safeguards and unequal access to specialised tools could weaken legitimacy, professional cohesion and access to justice. Nancarrow’s March 2025 preprint places greater emphasis on AI competing for professional jurisdiction and on the risk of unaccountable algorithmic governance. Its corporate-capture, hybrid-coexistence and public-reclamation futures are scenarios, not findings. Both approaches leave room for renewed professional roles, but distinguish successful adaptation from adequate protection of clients and the public.

qs.q: As we described, it rests on claims to serve the public interest, justified by a ‘regulative bargain’ in which professions are granted autonomy and social and financial rewards in return for ethical, competent service.
qs.a: Becoming, Doing, Being: GenAI and the Promise of Professional Identity in Law · Academia · 2025

qs.q: If left unchecked, AI could replace professional self-regulation with an opaque and unaccountable system of algorithmic governance, where neither human professionals nor the public have meaningful oversight.
qs.a: From Bureaucratic Closure to Algorithmic Governance: AI and the Neo-Weberian Crisis of the Professions · Academia · 2025

kps.k: The evidence supports situated accounts of change more strongly than sector-wide forecasts.
kps.d: The empirical core includes qualitative accounting and law research from 2018–2020, Augmented Lawyering’s interviews and surveys, a job-posting study available here only through its abstract, and the small fact-verification interview study. Earlier machine-learning findings cannot establish outcomes for later GenAI systems. Several contributions are theoretical syntheses or prospective frameworks, and many supplied excerpts contain only bibliographies, which add no substantive findings. Restricted data access and limited systematic practitioner evidence further qualify the account. The resulting research priority is to track tasks, staffing, expertise and governance over time across organisational and regulatory settings, without treating repeated citations or practitioner enthusiasm as independent confirmation.

qs.q: We draw on an original dataset collected between 2018 and 2020 comprising over 800 documents from the media and 80 interviews.
qs.a: Accommodating Machine Learning Algorithms in Professional Service Firms · Academia · 2024

qs.q: This Article presents what is to our knowledge the most comprehensive em-    pirical study yet conducted into the implementation of AI in legal services,    encompassing interview-based case studies and survey data.
qs.a: Augmented Lawyering · Academia · 2022

vlens.an: The supplied material for this professional voice does not permit a substantive comparison with the cluster’s proposition that AI redistributes legal tasks, status and professional power through organisational choices, boundary work and governance. The sole included source record is bibliographic rather than argumentative: it provides no claims, evidence or recommendations about task allocation, defended judgement domains, multidisciplinary influence, professional exclusivity, organisational form, learning or public accountability. Accordingly, it cannot be classified as supporting, extending, redirecting or opposing the proposition. Because the corpus is curated rather than a survey, this evidentiary gap should not be generalized to market analysts, consultancies or the press as a group.

The curated sources in the regulators, courts and professional-bodies voice do not provide enough substantive evidence to determine a collective position on the proposition that AI redistributes legal tasks and status through organisational choices and professional power. The OECD and legal-profession census excerpts consist only of bibliographic references: they identify topics such as workplace implementation, automation, surveillance and legal-AI performance, but disclose neither findings nor an institutional interpretation of their implications for professional boundaries, multidisciplinary influence or governance. The remaining source offers a fragmented assertion that humans remain in charge of technological innovation. That is broadly compatible with the proposition’s emphasis on human agency rather than technological determinism, but it does not explain how legal work, status or authority are redistributed. Thus, the limited internal variation runs from non-substantive research listings to a weakly aligned human-centred framing; none supplies a developed position for or against the cluster synthesis.

vlens.an: The substantively recoverable academic and research sources accept the proposition’s core claim and collectively develop it through concrete theories, empirical studies and governance frameworks. They explain AI-driven change as mediated by business models, partnership governance, professional autonomy and jurisdictional control; show how professionals can relinquish selected tasks while defending judgment-oriented work and creating new advisory domains; and trace how multidisciplinary collaboration can increase technologists’ status and influence within firms. Further extensions address externalised firm knowledge, professional identity and socialisation, risks to learning and interpretation, and public accountability. Material internal variation concerns emphasis and evidence: some sources offer interview, survey or job-posting evidence, whereas others are theoretical or prospective; some stress augmentation and renewed advisory value, while others foreground displacement, deskilling, occupational closure or algorithmic governance risks. Earlier 2018–2020 machine-learning findings do not establish later GenAI outcomes, and several sources explicitly treat employment and organisational futures as unsettled. Many other supplied records are bibliography-only and therefore remain uninformative rather than dissenting. Because this is a curated corpus, these convergences should not be treated as representative of academia generally or as evidence of prevalence.

qs.q: In particular, we highlight the central importance of business  models and organizational complements in mediating how AI affects the complex interplay of  task substitution, task augmentation, and the creation of new tasks.
qs.a: AI-enabled business models in legal services: from traditional law firms to next-generation law companies? · Academia · 2020

elens.an: The pre-2015 material neither supports nor challenges the proposition that AI redistributes legal tasks, status and professional power. The supplied excerpts from “What Is a Professional Service Firm? Toward a Theory and Taxonomy of Knowledge-Intensive Firms” are exclusively bibliographic entries and fragments; they disclose no substantive claims, evidence, reasoning or recommendations about AI, organisational choice, defended judgement domains, multidisciplinary collaboration or professional exclusivity. Titles in a reference list cannot establish which ideas the source accepts or how it applies them. Consequently, no common rationale or material internal variation can be identified for this period. This is an evidentiary limitation of the curated material, not evidence that pre-2015 scholarship lacked a position on the proposition.

The substantive 2015–2022 sources accept and materially develop the proposition that AI redistributes legal tasks and professional status through organisational arrangements and jurisdictional power, rather than technical capability alone. Their common move is away from whole-job replacement forecasts toward task-level substitution, augmentation and new multidisciplinary production roles. They explain outcomes through business-model complements, partnership or corporate governance, access to suitable human expertise, and professions’ ability to defend, delegate or share jurisdiction. Material variation concerns emphasis and evidential strength: Sako, Qian and Attolini provide a jurisdictional distinction between protective delegation and connective equal-status collaboration; Armour, Sako and Parnham focus on organisational fit and identify coordination of multidisciplinary teams as a central implementation problem; the AI-enhanced-lawyer account stresses selective automation and the increased relative value of human judgement; and Flood and Robb make the more prospective claim that even complex work may be automated while trusted advice becomes lawyers’ central value. Some supplied records are bibliography-only, so their positions are unclear and they add no substantive support or contradiction. Overall, this curated set builds on the proposition, but it does not establish sector-wide employment outcomes or a universally superior organisational form.

qs.q: Digital technology is a disturbance, and who ends up undertaking digital tasks depends on the nature of professional jurisdictional control.
qs.a: Future of professional work: evidence from legal jobs in Britain and the United States · Academia · 2022

qs.q: In particular, we highlight the central importance of business  models and organizational complements in mediating how AI affects the complex interplay of  task substitution, task augmentation, and the creation of new tasks.

elens.an: The substantive evidence available in this curated 2023–2024 set accepts the proposition that AI’s effects on legal work are mediated by organisational choices and professional power, and materially develops it through the concept of intertwined boundary work. Faulconbridge, Sarwar and Spring show professionals selectively moving routine work outside protected jurisdictions, defending judgement-oriented domains, creating new advisory work and negotiating collaboration with technologists; this collaboration can alter both divisions of labour and influence within professional service firms. Other substantive material supports the narrower pattern of substitution for repetitive, scalable tasks, augmentation of bespoke advice and creation of multidisciplinary work, while the accommodation framework similarly presents adoption as recursively controlled by professionals rather than technologically predetermined. Material variation concerns scope and evidential timing: the boundary-work and accommodation studies rely on qualitative evidence collected in 2018–2020, before the 2023–2024 generative-AI shock, and therefore illuminate organisational mechanisms more directly than later GenAI outcomes. The civil-justice source focuses more on capabilities and explainability constraints and less on governance, status or occupational power. Several other records are bibliography-only or fragmentary and are therefore Unclear rather than contrary evidence. The sources do not establish sector-wide employment effects, permanent human exclusivity or a single organisational outcome; they support situated reconfiguration more strongly than broad forecasts.

qs.q: By examining the adoption of AI in accounting and law professional service firms (PSFs), we show how professionals respond through intertwined boundary work, this being the process by which professionals respond to disruptions and protect interests and resources by engaging in multiple interdependent modes of boundary work.
qs.a: How Professionals Adapt to Artificial Intelligence: The Role of Intertwined Boundary Work · Academia · 2023

qs.q: Interdependencies between collaborative boundary work (negotiating) and configurational boundary work (coalescing) lead to changes to divisions of work and power structures in PSFs.
qs.a: How Professionals Adapt to Artificial Intelligence: The Role of Intertwined Boundary Work · Academia · 2023

elens.an: The substantive 2025 sources accept the proposition that AI’s effects on legal tasks and status are mediated by organisational choices, professional autonomy and struggles over expertise, and collectively extend it in material ways. Their common reasoning is that firms and professions actively determine which tasks are automated, which judgement domains remain defended, how multidisciplinary roles develop and who controls codified knowledge. The principal extensions are the externalisation of legal knowledge from individual lawyers into firm-held data, playbooks and AI systems, and the framing of AI as a competitor for professional jurisdiction that creates governance and public-accountability questions. Internal variation is substantial: Faulconbridge emphasises path-dependent, slow and compartmentalised adoption; Bell and Rogers focus on identity, socialisation, unequal access and the profession’s public bargain; the legal-knowledge archetype source considers both connective multidisciplinary professionalism and possible reductions in the number of broadly capable lawyers; Nancarrow gives greater weight to algorithmic governance and regulatory alternatives; and the narrower automation source mainly predicts that remedial work will shift to AI while lawyers retain higher-level analysis. Much of this evidence is theoretical, prospective or based on earlier machine-learning research, and several supplied records contain bibliographies only, so the period does not establish adoption at scale or settled employment outcomes. No substantive supplied source clearly opposes the proposition, but the curated selection should not be treated as representative of all 2025 commentary.

qs.q: Its capacity to codify, externalise, and convert that knowledge into data not only further reduces that vulnerability for firms; it starts to look transformative of both the business model and the individual role.
qs.a: The Evolution of Legal Knowledge Work in an Age of Brilliant(?) Technologies: From Robo-Lawyer to Digital Law Clerk · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Using Abbott’s System of Professions (1988) as a framework, we can see that AI is both disrupting professional domains while simultaneously competing for jurisdiction within them.
qs.a: From Bureaucratic Closure to Algorithmic Governance: AI and the Neo-Weberian Crisis of the Professions · Academia · 2025

elens.an: The usable 2026 material accepts the proposition that AI’s effects on legal work are organisational and sociological rather than technologically predetermined, and materially extends it. The principal contribution is a multilevel research agenda connecting human–AI interdependence with task redesign, tacit expertise, professional learning, technologists’ growing status, business models and governance. A small qualitative study of 18 legal professionals adds situated evidence that GenAI can reduce manual fact-verification work while influencing interpretation, responsibility and opportunities to develop professional intuition. Another source reinforces the proposition’s evidentiary caution by distinguishing practitioner reports of transformation from limited systematic evidence and potentially unreliable anecdotes. Internal variation is primarily one of scope and evidence: the research agenda develops broad theoretical mechanisms and open questions, whereas the interview study supplies narrow qualitative evidence and the legal-reasoning source chiefly qualifies stronger transformation claims. None establishes sector-wide deskilling, displacement or status change. Most other supplied records are bibliography-only excerpts, so their positions cannot be inferred; this evidentiary absence should not be interpreted as disagreement or used to estimate prevalence among 2026 sources.

qs.q: We argue that an approach is needed focused on emerging and future interdependencies between professionals and GML, something that implies extending but also reimagining theoretical perspectives on expertise, work, and organizations.
qs.a: Generative machine learning in professional work and professional service firms: a research agenda · Academia · 2026
